title: Polymer clay terrarium animal set
subtitle: Four miniature terrarium animals: snail, frog, butterfly, and hedgehog in polymer clay
excerpt: A terrarium animal set is four miniature polymer clay figures: a snail, a frog, a butterfly, and a hedgehog, each about 3-4 cm in their longest dimension and suited to sitting in a terrarium, on a windowsill plant pot, or in a display case. Polymer clay sets in a domestic oven, so no kiln is needed. Beginner makers who enjoy miniature work can complete all four figures in a single session.
sourceNotes: Miniature polymer clay animal figures technique derived from first principles.

content.text: A terrarium animal set is four miniature polymer clay figures, each between 3 and 4 cm across, designed to live in a plant terrarium, sit on a pot rim, or display on a shelf. Polymer clay sets in a domestic oven, so no kiln is needed. A beginner who enjoys small-scale work can finish all four figures in one sitting.

materials.name: Polymer clay, green (for frog, butterfly wing veins)
Polymer clay, brown or grey (for snail shell, hedgehog body)
Polymer clay, beige or cream (for snail body, hedgehog face)
Polymer clay, yellow and orange (for butterfly wings)
Polymer clay, black (for eyes, hedgehog spines, butterfly markings)
Polymer clay, white (for frog eyes, butterfly highlights)

content.text: Preparation
Condition all colours before sculpting:
conditioning

warms the clay and makes it smooth and easy to shape. Work each colour block between your palms, then fold and press it repeatedly until it bends without cracking at the fold. Condition black and white clays last to avoid contaminating pale colours with darker residue. Keep a clean tile or baking parchment sheet as your work surface.
Building the snail
Roll a log of beige clay about 6 cm long and 8 mm wide, tapering to a blunt point at one end for the tail. Bend the log gently into a shallow S curve. This is the snail body.

Shape the shell from brown clay: roll a rope 15 cm long and 5 mm wide, then coil it tightly in on itself from one end, spiralling outward. Press the coil gently together so it holds. This is the shell
armature
. Dome the top of the coil slightly by pressing with a fingertip.

Press the shell onto the back half of the body, blending the bottom edge of the shell into the body clay with a wooden rib so it sits securely. The shell should project upward and slightly to one side for a natural snail shape.

Add two tiny antenna stalks to the front of the head from thin ropes of beige clay. Top each with a small black ball eye pressed firmly onto the stalk tip. Use the needle tool to define the smile line under the head.
Building the frog

Roll an oval of bright green clay about 2.5 cm long for the body. Flatten it slightly so it sits without rocking. Shape two short back legs from small flattened ovals of the same green and press them out to either side of the body, blending the hip join with a wooden rib.

Roll two small front leg ropes about 1 cm long and press them to the front underside of the body, bending slightly outward. Press a small flat oval to the end of each leg for the front foot, using the needle tool to mark three toe lines.

Make the eyes from two small white balls pressed onto the top of the head at the corners. Press tiny black pupils onto each white ball. The eyes project upward from the head: a classic sitting frog shape.

Use the needle tool to draw a curved smile line across the face and to add fine cross-hatch texture to the back for a frog-skin effect. Press very lightly: deep marks in small figures become ragged when pressing so close to the surface.
Building the butterfly

Roll a thin black log about 3.5 cm long and taper both ends slightly for the body. Flatten two teardrop shapes from yellow or orange clay for the upper wings: each about 2 cm long. Flatten two smaller teardrops for the lower wings. Press all four wings to the sides of the body at the midpoint.
Press thin ropes of black clay along the wing edges and add a central vein on each wing.
Blend
the joins where the wings meet the body with a fingertip. Add small black dots to the upper wing surfaces using a tiny ball of black clay pressed flat.

Press two thin black antenna ropes to the top of the head, curving them outward and slightly upward. Top each with a tiny black or orange ball. Lay the butterfly flat for curing so the wings are supported.
Building the hedgehog
Roll an oval of grey or brown clay about 3 cm long for the body. Taper one end to a blunt point for the snout and keep the other end rounded. This profile gives the hedgehog its characteristic shape.

Cover the back two-thirds of the body (the rounded end) with tiny teardrop points of dark clay pressed in rows to simulate spines. Work from the base of the body upward in overlapping rows, pressing each point in firmly before placing the next. Each row of spines should partially cover the base of the row behind it.

Add a small beige or cream muzzle on the pointed end: a flattened oval about 8 mm across. Press two small black nostril dots with the tip of the needle tool. Add two small black eyes just above the muzzle edge.
Press four small flat oval feet to the base, two each side, at a slight outward angle. The hedgehog should sit flat and stable before curing.
Curing

Place all four figures on a tile or folded index card on the oven shelf. Cure at the temperature printed on the clay packaging, typically 110-130 degrees C, for 20-30 minutes. Miniature pieces with thin projections (antenna, leg tips) can scorch if the oven runs hot: use a digital thermometer to check the actual temperature. Remove and allow to cool fully on the tile before handling.
Finishing

After curing, add fine detail with a liner brush and acrylic paint. Paint the frog's belly a lighter green. Add orange-tipped antenna to the butterfly. Paint the hedgehog's nose dark brown. Seal the frog's skin with gloss varnish for a wet-look finish. Use matte varnish on the snail shell and hedgehog spines.
Care

These figures are decorative and not suitable for children under 3 due to small parts. Do not place in a microwave or dishwasher. Wipe with a dry cloth. Fine projections (antenna, legs) are the most fragile points: handle by the body, not the extremities.
Variations

Swap the butterfly for a ladybird: a round red body with black spots and black half-circle head. Ladybirds are easier to make than butterflies and a good first figure for beginners starting with the set.

Scale up the snail to 6 cm and add it to an outdoor container garden display: seal with several thick coats of outdoor varnish. Polymer clay resists water but direct soil contact will degrade any post-cure paint over time.

Extend the set to six or eight pieces by adding a bee (yellow and black striped oval with white wing flats) and a mouse (teardrop body, round ears, long pink tail rope). Use the same clay palette across all pieces for a coordinated set.
Troubleshooter

items.problem: Thin legs or antenna break on the frog or butterfly during handling
items.cause: The projections were too thin (under 2 mm) or were not fully bonded to the body before curing
items.fix: Re-attach post-cure with a tiny dot of superglue. For future figures, use slightly thicker ropes for projections and press the join firmly, blending with a wooden rib before curing

items.cause: The wings were unsupported in the oven and the softening clay relaxed under gravity
items.fix: Prop the wings at a slight upward angle using folded index card wedges under each wing tip before curing. Alternatively, cure the butterfly flat on the tile with wings pressed down

items.problem: Hedgehog spines look lumpy rather than pointy
items.cause: The spine pieces were too large or were not shaped to a fine enough tip before pressing onto the body
items.fix: Roll each spine piece into a sharper taper before pressing. Work with cooler clay for the spines: warm clay blunts faster under the heat of your fingers

items.problem: Colours bleed into each other at joins
items.cause: The adjacent clay pieces were blended too aggressively or the clay was over-conditioned and warm
items.fix: Chill the piece in the refrigerator for 5 minutes before adding the next colour. Use the needle tool rather than a fingertip to define the boundary between two colours
